8bb9c95ee7:
Task statement 5.3 asks for Opus vs Sonnet vs Haiku, adaptive thinking support, and breaking changes across releases. 5.4 asks for usage tracking, cost modelling, prompt caching and cache checkpointing. This chapter covers both.

You'll learn how to pick a model per step by measurement, and which thinking settings each current model accepts. There's a migration checklist. There's the usage record and the arithmetic that turns it into dollars. And there are the exact mechanics of prompt caching: how to keep a cache warm in a growing agent conversation, and how to prove it's working.
bade35baa3: Reading time: about 2.5 hours  ·  Companion code, 22 runnable examples: ccdvf-companion/15-model-selection-cost/ (run bash run_all.sh). Everything runs offline, using cachesim.py. That's a fake client that implements breakpoints, lookback, TTLs, minimum lengths, invalidating parameters and the usage fields.
1f5fcfe8e3: Neighbouring chapters: chapter 05 introduced the usage record. Chapter 07 owns the Batch API and batch-plus-cache arithmetic. Chapter 10 owns model-ID pinning. Chapter 13 owns what thinking and effort are. Chapter 16 owns context management. This chapter points to them rather than repeating them.
a325c09e97: Verified against the docs (October 2026): model list, prices, cache multipliers, minimums, lookback, invalidation table and migration guides. Prices change between releases. Treat every number here as "check the docs" before you put it in a real budget.
a6a0055c50:
Model choice is a per-step decision made by running your own eval on the cheapest candidate first and moving up (higher effort, then a larger tier) only when the measured quality falls short, and every model upgrade is a migration with breaking changes, not a string swap.

Cost is predictable from four usage counters priced at different rates, and prompt caching cuts the input side by up to 95% on reads, but only if the prefix up to each cache_control breakpoint is byte-for-byte identical between requests, long enough to be cached, and reused within its TTL.
e3767993c0:
At 5.5% of 53 items, this is about three direct questions. But cost and model choice show up as the deciding factor in many scenario stems: "the team wants to reduce cost without losing quality", "after upgrading the model, requests fail", "the cache hit rate is zero".

The distractors are predictable. Move everything to the biggest model. Cache the user's message. Put a timestamp in the system prompt. Or price only the answer text and forget the thinking tokens.
2bcb45b59a:
All current models share one API, one message format and one tool protocol. So changing tier means changing the model string, plus whatever the migration guide lists.

What differs is capability on hard tasks, latency, price per token, default thinking behaviour and a handful of accepted parameters. Treat tiers like instance sizes in a cloud fleet. You size each workload by measured load, not by habit.
99f2f847b8:
Four facts in this table carry exam weight.

  • The docs now say most workloads start on Opus 5.5 (capability-first). The alternative is efficiency-first on Haiku 5.5. "Start on Sonnet" was the older advice.
  • All four current models share a 1M-token context window and 128K max output. Context size is no longer a reason to choose a tier.
  • Haiku 5.5 is priced per request by prompt length. A request whose total input (including cache reads and writes) exceeds 100K tokens pays five times the rate on every token.
  • Opus 5.5 and Fable 5.1 always think. You can't turn thinking off, only lower effort.

The Models API (GET /v1/models/{id}) returns max_input_tokens, max_tokens and a capabilities object. So code can check support (for example capabilities.thinking.types.disabled.supported) instead of hard-coding it.
e20e185b95:
Be precise about what a tier change does not change. Several distractors rely on the opposite belief.

The request and response shapes are identical across tiers. A client library, a tool registry, a streaming parser and a usage logger written for one model work for all of them. Tool use, structured outputs, vision, PDF input, citations and prompt caching are available on all four current models. The context window and the maximum output are the same.

What changes is this: the model's skill on hard problems, the time it takes per token, the price per token, the default thinking and effort behaviour, a few accepted parameter values, and cache minimums and read multipliers.

In Java terms, the API is a stable interface with four implementations whose performance contracts differ. Your code depends on the interface. The choice of implementation is configuration.
b40f41fb7c:
The parameter differences are real. Section 06 shows requests that are valid on one model and a 400 on the next. So hard-coding "if model starts with claude-opus then ..." in a request builder is a mistake. It's the same mistake as hard-coding a database vendor check in business code.

The Models API exposes the facts. A gateway can read them once at startup and build requests from data. The field names below are as documented in October 2026. Check the docs for the full capabilities shape before you depend on a specific key.
1fb3ad594c:
The same principle works in the other direction. Say a team evaluates a model and finds it fails on a step. The useful question is "which capability is missing, measured how?", not "which tier is it?".

Two answers matter in practice. If the failure is reasoning depth (multi-step diagnosis, long code changes, judgement across many constraints), higher effort or a larger tier helps. If the failure is missing knowledge (a product catalogue, today's outage list, a customer's contract), no tier helps. The fix is retrieval or a tool.

Picking a larger model to fix a knowledge gap is one of the most expensive mistakes in this domain. It's also a recurring exam distractor.
41070f1453: The procedure the docs recommend is empirical, and it's the one the exam rewards. Opinions about which model is "smart enough" are worth nothing next to an eval of your prompts on your data.
405908ef4c: Pick a starting strategy. Capability-first: get it right on Opus 5.5, then lower effort or move down while the eval holds. Efficiency-first: start on Haiku 5.5, and upgrade only where a measured gap appears.
6ccd0209c1: Turn the effort dial before the tier dial. Raising effort on the same model buys reasoning for the requests that need it. Changing tier raises the price of every token.
c8606ee869:
Per-step routing is where the money is. Take a telecom order-fallout assistant. Triage is classification, and Haiku 5.5 passes. Diagnosis reasons over order history and inventory, and Opus 5.5 may be the only model that meets the bar. The customer reply is writing, so Sonnet 5.5.

Companion example 12 runs this. It evaluates each step from the cheapest model up and stops at the first that meets the bar. Then it prints the resulting route and its cost per conversation against an all-Opus design.
0e4e074db5:
The docs describe two multi-model shapes that the exam may name. An orchestrator on a frontier model delegates bulk work to cheaper workers (the subagent pattern from chapter 03). An executor on a cheaper model escalates hard decisions to an advisor on a frontier model. Both put most tokens on the cheap model.

A static router like the one above is enough when the steps are known. The next step up is a learned or rule-based router that inspects each request ("long contract, escalate"). That router needs its own eval for misroutes.
697c8ebd2f:
Latency is the other selection criterion. Haiku is fastest per token. But the latency a user sees on a reasoning task is dominated by how many tokens get generated, thinking included. So a lower effort on a larger model can beat a higher effort on a smaller one.

Opus 5.5 also offers fast mode (research preview, speed: "fast"). It gives up to about 2.5x output speed at $8 / $40 per MTok, and it isn't available in batch. Streaming (chapter 06) improves perceived latency without changing cost.
a60314558e:
The procedure in section 03 is easy to agree with and easy to skip. The four cases below run it end to end on workloads with different shapes. The shape decides which number dominates the answer: price per call, price per successful outcome, throughput price, or latency.

Each case states its unit of work, its quality bar and any hard constraint. Then it prices every candidate that could pass. The accuracies and latencies are illustrative stand-ins for your own eval results. The prices are the October 2026 list prices, and the arithmetic is exact. Companion example 16 reproduces every number, so you can swap in your own inputs.
fac6762827: A shared notation keeps the arithmetic short. A call has a stable prefix of S tokens, cached with hit rate h. It has a dynamic part of D tokens, and O output tokens including thinking. Its cost in dollars is [S × (h·r + (1−h)·1.25) + D] × P_in + O × P_out, divided by a million, and halved for batch. Every case below is this formula with different numbers.
2421ce8d0e:
A mobile operator's support assistant handles plan changes, roaming questions and bill explanations. It runs 300,000 conversations a month, five calls each, so 1.5 million calls.

Each call carries an 8,000-token prefix (tool definitions, the policy handbook, a few worked examples) and about 2,000 tokens of conversation. It writes a 300-token reply. With a moving checkpoint, the prefix hit rate is about 90%.

The quality bar is "92% of answers policy-correct" on a 400-case eval graded against the handbook. There's no hard latency constraint beyond normal chat expectations.
0726d830fc:
Three things in this table matter more than the verdict.

First, the gap between Sonnet at low and at high effort is entirely thinking tokens. The visible reply is the same 300 tokens. The extra 1,200 thinking tokens at $10 per million double the bill. Leaving a model at its default effort is a decision, and usually an unexamined one.

Second, Haiku fails by four points. Before you accept a 17x higher bill, section 03's order says to try the prompt first. Suppose the failures cluster on one policy area (say roaming credit rules). Adding two worked examples for that area may lift Haiku over the bar. Those examples sit in the cached prefix, so they cost almost nothing per call.

Third, a hybrid is available. Route the policy areas where Haiku passes to Haiku, and the rest to Sonnet (section 05). That option is only visible if the eval is stratified by policy area. That's why section 03 insisted on stratification.
b73f370af7:
An internal agent fixes defects in an order-management code base. It handles 4,000 tasks a month, at about 40 turns per attempt. The context grows to well over 100K tokens and averages about 60K. Most of each turn's input is the cached history (92% hit rate with a moving checkpoint). Each turn produces about 1,500 output tokens, thinking included.

Here the unit of work isn't a call, and it isn't even an attempt. It's a resolved task. A failed attempt still costs its tokens. It also costs an engineer about 30 minutes to notice, diagnose and redo, priced here at $45.
d3d818d848:
The cheapest model per token is the most expensive per outcome. That's the general shape of agentic work. Token cost per attempt is small next to the cost of a failure, so a few points of success rate outweigh a doubling of token price.

The formula to remember is (attempt cost + failure rate × failure cost) / success rate. It also explains why raising effort on Opus lowered the cost per resolved task again, even though it costs more per attempt. The docs' advice to start agentic coding on Opus 5.5 is this arithmetic in prose.

Some task sets have a long tail of genuinely hard cases where even Opus at high effort fails. Then Fable 5.1 enters the comparison on the same formula, not on reputation.
1fa96564c2:
A billing operations team extracts 14 fields from 2 million scanned invoices and contracts a month. They're already OCR'd to text, about 3,000 tokens each. There's a 1,200-token instruction and schema prefix, and about 400 output tokens of JSON.

Nobody waits for an individual result. The downstream reconciliation runs at 06:00. That deadline is the most important fact in the case. It makes the Batch API (chapter 07) eligible, and batch halves every token category, cache reads and writes included.
ae13b6c631:
Haiku passes, so the choice between Haiku options comes down to the deadline. Batch wins by half. Two details trip people up.

The first is the cache minimum. The instruction prefix is 1,200 tokens, comfortably above the 512-token minimum of the 5.x generation, so it caches. On Haiku 4.5 (minimum 4,096), the same prefix would silently not cache at all. That difference alone is worth checking in any older cost model.

The second is the hit rate. In batch it's lower and less predictable than in realtime traffic, because batch requests run in an order you don't control, over a long window. The model assumes 80% rather than 95%, and the 1-hour TTL improves the odds (chapter 07).

A one-point accuracy gain from Sonnet is worth $16,000 a month only if a missed field costs more than about $0.80 to fix by hand. The decision is a business number. The exam expects you to ask for it, not to assume "more accurate is better".
8bfa3ad259:
An IVR front end classifies a transcribed caller utterance into one of 30 intents while the caller waits. That's 30 million calls a month. Each has a 1,200-token cached prompt (intent list with descriptions and examples), about 300 tokens of utterance, and a five-token answer.

The latency limit is a hard constraint, and that changes the procedure. Candidates that miss it are out, whatever their price or accuracy. Latency is dominated by time to first token plus generated tokens divided by output speed. Thinking tokens are generated tokens. The latency model below (250 ms to first token, 200 tokens per second) is illustrative. Measure p95 on your own traffic.
c377d45b60:
This case is where the thinking support matrix (section 06) becomes a selection criterion. Opus 5.5 always thinks. That makes it structurally unsuited to a 700 ms budget, no matter how good it is. Haiku 5.5 can disable thinking at effort high or below, which keeps generated tokens at five.

The other levers for this shape are caching the intent list and keeping the output tiny. Cache reads cut time to first token as well as cost. A strict schema or a single-token label keeps the output small. Fast mode is the wrong tool here. It raises output speed on Opus, but five tokens aren't the bottleneck, and it doubles the price.
8f0a1d7021:
Case A ended with "route some policy areas to Haiku and the rest to Sonnet". Once a system uses more than one model per step, the question becomes: how does a request find its model?

There are four designs. They differ in who decides, when, and on what evidence. The exam tends to describe a symptom ("costs are high but 80% of requests are simple") and ask for the design. So know what each one costs, and how each one fails.
4e68f33d50:
A static map is section 03's output. It's the right answer whenever the steps are known and homogeneous.

A classifier router adds a decision before the work. That can be a regular expression, a feature rule ("contracts longer than 50 pages go to Opus") or a Haiku call that labels difficulty. It pays the router's cost on every request. It also needs its own eval, because its errors are invisible in aggregate accuracy.

Here's how that hides. If the router sends 5% of hard requests to the small model, and the small model gets half of those wrong, overall accuracy drops by 2.5 points. Nobody sees why unless misroutes are logged and sampled.
67d7fbd4bc:
A cascade sends every request to the cheap model first. It escalates only when a check on the answer fails. Its expected cost is csmall + pesc × clarge. So it beats "always large" whenever the escalation rate is below 1 − csmall/clarge. With Haiku 5.5 in front of Sonnet 5.5, that's any escalation rate below about 95%.

The whole design rests on the check. With a check that catches most wrong answers, a cascade gets close to the large model's quality at a fraction of its cost. With a check that misses wrong answers, it ships the small model's errors, plus extra latency.
db26eee079:
The most common broken check is the model's own confidence. You ask the small model "how confident are you, high or low?" and escalate on "low". It looks reasonable. It doesn't work.

Verbalised confidence is only weakly related to correctness, and a model that's wrong is usually wrong confidently. Chapter 18's output-handling material makes the same point about trusting confident output.

The fixed version escalates on evidence the code can check:

  • the output parses against the schema;
  • required fields are present;
  • values pass business rules (the plan code exists, the credit is under the policy limit, the dates are in order);
  • a second extraction of a key field agrees;
  • a retrieval check finds the cited clause.

Companion example 17 simulates both gates on 20,000 order-change requests.
f8c7322036:
The advisor and orchestrator shapes from section 03 move the decision inside the model. A Sonnet or Haiku executor calls an "ask the expert" tool backed by Opus when it judges a decision hard. Or an Opus orchestrator hands bulk sub-tasks to Haiku workers (chapter 03's subagent pattern).

These are the most flexible designs and the hardest to evaluate, because the escalation decision is itself model output. Treat it the way you treat the cascade's gate. Log every escalation, and every non-escalation on a sample. Grade whether the decision was right. And cap escalations per task, so a confused executor can't route everything to the expensive model.
f97af1c182:
For a Spring architect, routing is a familiar pattern with an unfamiliar cost structure.

  • A static map is a Map<Step, ModelConfig> bound from configuration.
  • A classifier router is a RoutingDataSource-style strategy chosen per request.
  • A cascade is a chain of responsibility with a validator between links. It's close to a Resilience4j fallback, except the fallback triggers on bad content, not on an exception.

The difference from routing database traffic is that the target's correctness varies per request, not just its availability. So every router needs an eval of its routing decisions, not only of the models behind it.
33cbcb0305:
Chapter 13 explains what thinking and effort are. For selection and migration you need the support matrix, because the same request can be valid on one model and a 400 on the next.

The current generation uses adaptive thinking. The model decides per request whether to think and how much. You steer it with output_config.effort (low, medium, high, xhigh, max). There's no thinking budget. Cost is controlled by effort and by max_tokens, which covers thinking plus text.
fac44f81b3:
Three consequences follow.

Cost: thinking tokens are billed as output tokens even when the thinking text isn't shown. display controls visibility, not billing. So a request with a 300-token answer and 4,000 tokens of thinking pays for 4,300 output tokens. usage.output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens tells you how many.

Parsing: responses may start with a thinking block even when you didn't ask for one. Read content blocks by type.

Steering: on Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5, telling the model in the prompt to "answer directly" doesn't reliably stop thinking. Lower the effort instead.

Companion example 13 prices the same visible answer at three effort levels. It shows the naive estimate (answer length only) undercounting by up to 14x.
4dcab3eb5e: A model upgrade looks like a one-line config change. It behaves like a dependency major-version bump. The migration guides for Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5 and Haiku 5.5 group their changes by the model you start from. The ones below either break requests (HTTP 400) or silently change cost or output. Each is a line in your migration checklist.
3312022fba:
The list will be different for the next release. The exam tests the habit, not the rows.

The habit is a checklist you run before every model change. Read the migration guide for your starting model. Lint requests against it. Recount tokens with the new tokenizer. Rerun the eval. Compare cost per task. Then roll out behind a flag, with the old pinned ID as the rollback.

And note that aliases move. A floating alias can change models under you. That's why chapter 10 insists on pinned IDs in production.
db35544ef4:
The table in section 07 is a catalogue. A migration is a sequence. This section walks through one on a realistic service, so the order of the steps, and the reason for each, is clear.

The service is case C's ancestor: an invoice extraction endpoint built a year ago on claude-haiku-4-5. It uses temperature: 0 "for determinism", a 1,024-token thinking budget, and a prefilled { to force JSON. It works. The team wants Haiku 5.5's price and accuracy, and the change ticket says "update model ID".

Here's what the Haiku 5.5 migration guide (verified October 2026) says will happen, starting from Haiku 4.5.
fdff51bcab:
Notice the structure. Three items break every request, loudly. The rest change cost, output shape or rare branches, quietly. A team that fixes the 400s and ships has done a third of the migration.

The remaining steps exist for the quiet items. They're the same steps whatever the model pair.
518f51c89f: Inventory. Find every call site and the request shapes it produces. Logged requests (with prompts redacted as policy requires) make the best inventory. They show what the code actually sends once all the configuration is applied.
806bfaca49: Lint. Run every logged request shape through a linter that encodes the guide (companion example 14 and example 18). The linter turns the guide into a failing test. That's how a Java team would treat a deprecated API after a framework upgrade.
e2e4bb56b2: Recount. Use the token counting endpoint with the new model ID on a sample of real prompts. Update context-budget checks, max_tokens and the cost model with the measured ratio, not with the guide's approximate 30%.
9f072e25c2: Replay the eval. Run the same stratified eval through both pinned IDs. Compare quality per stratum, cost per document, latency, stop-reason distribution and cache counters. New refusal and max_tokens stops are a signal.
5b48c8cc07: Canary. Ship behind a flag to a small share of traffic, with the old pinned ID as the rollback. Watch the same metrics live, then ramp.
661aa6b6e9: Clean up. Once the old model is no longer the rollback target, remove the old code path and the flag. Record the new baseline (quality, cost, hit rate) for the next migration.
4d60e87dc7:
In example 18 the replay reports 94.5% accuracy at $0.0080 per document on Haiku 4.5, and 96.5% at $0.00065 on Haiku 5.5. There are 30% more tokens, but the price per token is one tenth as large. And low effort thinks less than the old 1,024-token budget did. (The accuracies are simulated. The token-ratio and price effects are the real ones.) The gate passes, so the rollout proceeds to a canary.

Suppose the team had gated on cost from the guide's price table alone. They'd have missed the tokenizer effect. That effect matters a great deal for any model pair with closer prices, such as a Sonnet generation change. There, a 30% token increase can turn an expected saving into a cost increase.
c55ffe6fd6:
The Java parallel is a framework major-version upgrade, such as Spring Boot 2 to 3. A migration guide lists removed properties and changed defaults. OpenRewrite-style recipes apply the mechanical changes. The test suite catches the loud breaks. Performance testing catches the quiet ones, like a changed connection-pool default that only shows under load.

The difference is that a model's quiet changes are in output quality and token counts. So the "test suite" is an eval, and the "performance test" is a cost replay. Teams that already run contract tests and canary releases for service upgrades have the habits. They only need to add those two measurements.
36e771d9b0:
Two more migration points come up often enough to know.

Aliases versus pinned IDs: an alias that moves to a new model performs this whole migration on the vendor's schedule, without the gate. That's why production code pins (chapter 10).

Deprecation timelines: models are deprecated, then retired on published dates, after which requests fail. A migration started the week of retirement has no time for a replay or a canary. So the deprecation notice is the trigger to start, not the retirement date. Check the docs' model deprecations page for current dates.
54a6a48e10: Every response carries a usage object. It's your billing record, your capacity record and your cache telemetry. And it's exact, unlike any client-side token estimate.
b191362b1b:
The trap is input_tokens. Without caching, it's the whole input. With caching, it's only the part after the last breakpoint.

Total input = cache_read_input_tokens + cache_creation_input_tokens + input_tokens.

A dashboard that plots input_tokens shows a 99% drop in "input" the day caching ships. A context-window check that uses it will let a conversation run into the limit. Example 04 shows a request whose input_tokens is 27 while the model processed 8,027.
4dd20e7584:
Output works the other way. output_tokens is the authoritative total and already includes thinking, so don't add thinking_tokens on top.

If both cache counters are zero on a request you meant to cache, it wasn't cached. Section 19 lists the usual signatures. Server tools add their own counters; web search requests, for example, are billed per search, $10 per 1,000. Check the docs for the current field names.

On every call, log the four counters, the model, the request id and a feature tag.
57c4cec194: Take per-MTok prices Pin and Pout. Take a cache read multiplier r: 0.05 on Opus 5.5 and Sonnet 5.5, 0.1 on Haiku, 0.025 on Fable 5.1. And take write multipliers of 1.25 (5-minute) and 2 (1-hour). The cost of one call is:
d0ea7f4c89:
The multipliers stack.

  • Batch halves everything, cache rates included.
  • US-only data residency (inference_geo: "us", Claude 4.6 and later) multiplies every category by 1.1.
  • Haiku 5.5 switches to its higher rate table for any request whose total input exceeds 100K.

On Claude 4.6 and later (except Haiku 5.5), long context has no surcharge. A 900K-token request costs the same per token as a 9K one. Tools add a fixed system-prompt overhead per request: 286 tokens on Opus and Sonnet 5.5.
cf8d7e306a: Take 2 million conversations a month, 4 calls each, so 8 million calls. Each call sends a 6,000-token stable prefix (tools, system prompt, policy) and 900 tokens of conversation. It produces 250 output tokens. On Sonnet 5.5 at $2 / $10:
848c33177e:
Three lessons. Caching the prefix cuts this bill by about two thirds. That's more than any tier change short of Haiku. Thinking tokens at the output rate can erase that saving, so effort belongs in the cost model. And the largest lever is still the model. That's why the eval in section 03 comes first.

Companion example 02 reproduces the table. Change the inputs to model your own workload.
537751f28f:
The support-assistant table priced one call shape. Real systems mix shapes: a cheap classifier, a multi-turn agent, a writing step and an offline job. Each runs on its own model, cache layout and pricing mode.

A monthly estimate for a system like that is built line by line. Each line comes from a realistic usage record, not from averages. Averages hide exactly the things that dominate: a growing agent context, thinking tokens, the cold first call of each cache window.

This section builds one for a telecom order-fallout assistant. Orders that fail provisioning land in a queue. The assistant triages them, diagnoses the cause with tools, and drafts the customer message. Overnight, it summarises every case for the operations report.
d84e97b66b:
The method is to simulate one unit per line item in steady state, price its usage records, then multiply by volume.

Steady state matters. The first diagnose conversation after a quiet hour writes the 9K prefix at 2x. But the 1-hour entry is shared by every case in that hour. So its write is amortised across hundreds of cases, and the typical case reads it.

Companion example 19 does exactly this with the caching simulator. The per-turn cache reads and writes of the agent loop come from the same rules as section 16's trace, not from a guessed hit rate.
dbdb95a092:
The table answers the question every cost review should start with: where is the money? Here 93% of spend is one line, the agent loop. Optimisation effort belongs there and nowhere else. Moving triage from Haiku to anything cheaper, or tuning the nightly batch, changes the total by less than rounding.

Within the agent line, here are the levers, biggest first:

  • Caching, already applied. Without it the line is 3.75x larger.
  • The model. Sonnet 5.5 has exactly half Opus 5.5's prices on every category. If the diagnosis eval passes on Sonnet, the line halves to about $9,800.
  • The number of turns. Each turn re-reads the whole history. A tool that returns a 300-token summary instead of an 1,800-token record cuts every later turn.
  • Effort. 300 thinking tokens per turn at $20 per million is $0.048 per case.
550b0db302:
Each assumption in the model also becomes a monitoring target after launch.

  • The 5% retry allowance becomes an alert on retries per call.
  • The 60% batch hit rate becomes a weekly check of batch cache counters.
  • The 8 turns become a histogram of turns per case. Its tail is where runaway agents show up.
  • The 300 thinking tokens become a dashboard of thinking_tokens by step.

A forecast whose assumptions aren't monitored can't be falsified. The first sign that it was wrong will be the invoice.
00fa3a1d98:
A spreadsheet is fine for the arithmetic. The discipline is in the inputs. Each line should state its unit, its source (eval run, production sample or guess), and the date of the price table used. When the pricing page changes, or a migration shifts token counts by 30%, you update the model in one place.

For an architect, this is the same artefact as a capacity plan for a new service. It's a per-request resource profile multiplied by forecast volume. The assumptions are written down, so operations can tell which one broke when reality diverges.
ddd0cb86ba:
A cost model is a forecast. Usage tracking is the measurement that confirms or refutes it.

The minimum is a wrapper around every model call. It records the usage counters with enough labels to answer "which feature, which model, which tenant, which prompt version spent this?".

The organisation-level views aggregate by workspace, model and API key. Those are the Console usage and cost pages, and the Admin API usage and cost report endpoints (check the docs for current paths). But they can't see your features or tenants. Separate workspaces or API keys per product give coarse attribution for free. Per-call logging gives the rest.
61aa247353:
In a Spring service, the same idea is a decorator or Micrometer instrumentation around the client. You get counters llm.tokens{kind=input|cache_read|cache_write|output, model, feature} and a cost gauge, exported to Prometheus, with alerts on cost per feature per hour.

With the Anthropic Java SDK, the counters are on message.usage(). The cache fields are optional values, with method names such as cacheReadInputTokens(). Check the SDK reference.
c0269c0ace:
Three practices separate useful tracking from logging for its own sake.

Budget per unit of work. Alert on cost per conversation or per resolved ticket, not just per day. An agent stuck in a tool loop shows up there first.

Count before you send where it matters. The token counting endpoint returns the input token count for a request without running it. A gateway can use that to reject or trim oversized requests. (Counts can differ slightly from the final usage.)

Reconcile your per-call totals with the organisation cost report weekly. A gap means some code path bypasses the wrapper.
376b7f879c:
At production volume, the wrapper is the first stage of a small data pipeline. Each stage exists because it answers a question the previous one can't.

  • The wrapper emits one usage event per call. That has to be cheap on the request path: an append to a queue, never a blocking database write.
  • A stream processor aggregates events into metrics (tokens and dollars per minute by model, feature and tenant) for dashboards and alerts.
  • The raw events land in a warehouse table, for questions nobody thought of in advance. "What did the March prompt change do to cost per resolved ticket for enterprise tenants?"
  • A weekly reconciliation job compares warehouse totals with the organisation cost report from the Console or Admin API.

Any gap above a few percent means one of three things. A code path calls the API without the wrapper. A retry storm happened that the wrapper didn't see. Or a price table is out of date.
cfd6a1d32e:
The event schema deserves the same care as any API contract. Changing it later breaks every dashboard. Useful fields beyond the usage counters:

  • conversation or task id, for cost per unit of work;
  • step name, for which part of a multi-step pipeline;
  • prompt version (chapter 10's versioned prompts), so a cost jump can be tied to a prompt change;
  • effort and thinking mode, the most common silent cost driver;
  • stop reason, since a rising share of max_tokens stops is lost money;
  • attempt number, since retries are spend with no extra value;
  • batch flag and price table version.

Prompt text and outputs usually don't belong in this stream. They have different retention and privacy rules (chapter 19). Keep them in a separate trace store keyed by request id.
8c1750edd4:
A dashboard tells you yesterday's cost. A budget has to act before the money is spent, and the order of operations decides whether it can.

The broken version checks the running total after each call. The call that crosses the line is already paid for. And if the check lives in a nightly report, an agent stuck in a tool loop runs all day.

The fixed version reserves the worst-case cost of the next call before sending it: counted input priced at full rate, plus max_tokens at the output rate. If the reservation would exceed the budget, it refuses the call. Afterwards, it settles the reservation to the actual usage cost.

This is the same reserve-then-settle pattern as a credit authorisation in a billing system. It gives a hard ceiling, because the worst case bounds the real cost.
28a616f15d:
In example 20, an Opus agent that keeps asking for the same lookup runs 60 turns and spends $1.73 unguarded. With a $0.50 per-conversation budget, it stops cleanly before turn 16, at $0.34.

Three budget scopes cover most systems.

  • Per unit of work (conversation, task, document) catches loops and pathological inputs. Size it at a high percentile of the measured distribution, not the mean.
  • Per tenant per day protects the business from one customer's automation, and maps to commercial limits.
  • Per feature per hour catches regressions, such as a prompt change that doubled thinking.

Each needs a defined action when it's hit: end the agent with a message to the user, queue for human review, or degrade to a cheaper model. Choose the action per feature in advance, not at 2am.
06020a5a0c:
Budgets catch the big failures. The slow ones are caught by anomaly alerts.

Compare cost per unit of work against a rolling baseline for the same feature, and alert at a multiple of it. Example 20 uses 4x the rolling mean. Separately, alert on the inputs to cost: token hit rate (section 19), thinking tokens per call, turns per task and retries per call.

A cost anomaly with all four inputs normal means traffic grew. That's a capacity conversation, not an incident.
0c4061c28e:
Most requests in a real application repeat the same long beginning: tool definitions, a system prompt, a policy document, few-shot examples, and, in a conversation, every previous turn. Processing that prefix is the expensive part of input.

Prompt caching stores the model's processed state for a prefix. It reuses that state when a later request starts with exactly the same tokens. You pay a premium to write the entry and a small fraction to read it. Reads are also faster, with a lower time to first token.
61d70e91bb:
The rules follow from what is cached. The state at the end of a prefix depends on every token before it. So the cache key is effectively a hash of the whole prefix, in the order the API renders it: tools, then system, then messages.

Change one character anywhere, and every entry that covers that position becomes a different key. Hits need a 100% identical prefix up to the cached point. That's why stable content goes first and volatile content goes last. It's also why a changed tool definition, which sits at the very start, invalidates everything.
c253b1de49:
You don't need the server's implementation to reason about caching. You need a model that predicts its behaviour. The one that works is a hash chain, the structure behind git commits and blockchain ledgers.

Walk the rendered prompt block by block and keep a running hash: h0 = H(model), hi = H(hi−1 ‖ blocki). Each hi identifies the entire prefix up to block i. So it can serve as the key of a cache entry holding the model's processed state at that point.

A breakpoint at block i means "store the state under key hi". A later request computes its own chain and looks for its keys in the store.
94af7de72d:
Every caching rule in this chapter falls out of that picture.

  • Exact match: one changed character in block 2 changes h2, and therefore every later h. Nothing from block 2 on can match. h1 is unchanged and can still hit.
  • Order matters: the same blocks in a different order produce a different chain. A tool list built from a set misses.
  • Position decides damage: tools render first, so a tool edit changes every key. A new user turn at the end changes no existing key.
  • Model-scoped: the chain starts from the model, so entries don't carry across models. A router that alternates models per request gets two separate caches. (This is how caching behaves in practice; check the docs if a design depends on it.)
  • Parameters as content: some settings are rendered into the prompt, such as thinking configuration, effort, tool_choice, fast mode or a web search toggle. They act like hidden blocks at a fixed position. That's why each one invalidates exactly the segments after the position where it's rendered.
  • Writes only at breakpoints: the store holds states only at keys someone asked to store. So a later request can only hit at a position where an earlier request placed a breakpoint. That's why the lookback window in section 14 exists. It lets a new breakpoint find an older key a few blocks earlier.
2e4500cef6:
Two consequences are easy to miss.

First, the hash covers rendered content. Two requests that look the same in your code can differ on the wire. A dictionary gets serialised with a different key order. A float prints as 1.0 once and 1 once. An image is re-encoded with different compression. Whitespace is normalised by one code path and not another. When a cache misses for no visible reason, diff the serialised request bytes, not the source objects.

Second, thinking blocks that the model returns and you pass back in history are part of the chain like any other block. If your code strips, reorders or re-serialises them, the chain breaks at that point (section 15).
4ae6ce27bf:
Explicit breakpoints go on individual blocks: a tool definition, a system text block, or a content block in a message. You get up to four per request. Each one writes an entry for the prefix ending at that block.

Automatic caching is a single top-level cache_control on the request. The API places the breakpoint on the last cacheable block and moves it forward as the conversation grows. It uses one of the four slots. It's a no-op if the last block already has the same explicit marker. It's a 400 if the TTLs conflict or four explicit breakpoints already exist.

(On the legacy Bedrock integration for Opus 4.6 and earlier, top-level cache_control is a 400. Use explicit breakpoints there.)
4aa9d9f4c3:
How reads find entries matters for long conversations. Writes happen only at breakpoints. Reads look backward from each breakpoint, checking up to 20 block positions for an entry an earlier request wrote. The breakpoint itself is the first. Consecutive tool_use blocks count as one position, and so do consecutive tool_result blocks. If the window finds nothing, that breakpoint gets no hit.

So a conversation can miss even though the old prefix is still cached. That happens when it adds more than about 20 blocks between requests, or when its previous entry has scrolled out of the window. A second, earlier breakpoint fixes it, because each breakpoint has its own window. Example 10 shows both cases.
f3a56e03c3: The key is the rendered prefix. So some request parameters that look unrelated to the prompt are rendered into it. Here's the docs' invalidation table, condensed:
1d43a29ad2:
The common self-inflicted misses aren't in the table, because they're your own content:

  • a timestamp, request id or user name at the top of the system prompt;
  • tools assembled from a set or dict in non-deterministic order;
  • JSON serialised with unstable key order;
  • a per-tenant greeting interpolated before the shared policy;
  • editing earlier history (summarising or trimming old turns), which rewrites the prefix from that point.

The fix is always the same. Stable content first. Volatile content after the last breakpoint. Deterministic serialisation.
57eb504cbe:
Some agents must change tools or instructions mid-conversation. For them, the docs describe two escape hatches that avoid rewriting the prefix.

  • Append a {"role": "system"} message inside messages instead of editing the top-level system. This is supported on the 5.5 models and some others.
  • Send a new tool in a tool_addition block under a beta header, and leave tools unchanged.

Both are new. Check the docs for current support before relying on them in an exam answer. There, "keep tools and system stable" is the safe principle.
9c6ed412d7:
Four details from the prompt-caching docs (verified October 2026) refine the table. A scenario can hinge on any of them.

Explicit default effort is free: setting output_config.effort explicitly to the model's default is the same as omitting it, and doesn't invalidate. So a code change from "omit effort" to "effort: medium" on Opus 5.5 is safe. The same change on Sonnet 5.5 (default high) invalidates the messages cache once.

"Model-specific" for thinking and effort means the configuration is always rendered before the messages. On some models it's also rendered before tools and system. Then changing it costs the whole prefix. Plan as if it does.

Thinking blocks across user turns: on Opus 4.5 and later, Sonnet 4.6 and later and Haiku 5.5, previous thinking blocks are preserved when you add ordinary user content, so the cache stays valid. Earlier models (including Haiku 4.5) behave differently. Adding non-tool-result user content strips earlier thinking blocks from context and invalidates the cache from there. That made multi-turn thinking conversations cache poorly on those models.

Cached thinking counts as input: thinking blocks read back from cache are billed and counted as input tokens, at the read rate. So long thinking-heavy histories grow the input side too.
1f12c0a06c:
The table also has a counterpart for request validity, not just cache validity. On Haiku 5.5, sending a thinking block back after changing system, tools or earlier messages is a 400. Per the migration guides, the same goes for other 5.5 models on accounts created after a cut-off date.

That turns "edit history and accept one cache miss" into "edit history and fail". It's why the guides say to keep conversations append-only. It's also why compaction (chapter 16) should produce a new conversation rather than rewrite an old one in place. Check the docs for the exact cut-off and opt-in field before relying on either behaviour.
0030a43323:
Rules are easiest to trust once you've watched them operate on one conversation, turn by turn. Companion example 21 runs a twelve-turn Opus 5.5 diagnosis agent with three breakpoints:

  • T on the last tool definition (1-hour TTL);
  • S on the system runbook (1-hour TTL, about 4,000 tokens);
  • M, the automatic moving checkpoint on the last block (5-minute TTL).

Each turn appends a tool_use block and a roughly 700-token tool_result. Six events are injected on purpose. Each is a mistake or a legitimate change seen in real agents. The counters below are what the usage record reports for each request.
d45c9d1302:
Read the table for its prices, not just its patterns.

At Opus 5.5 rates, a steady turn such as turn 8 costs about 9,185 × $0.20 + 735 × $5.00 per million. That's roughly $0.0055 of input. Turn 9, after the tool edit, costs at least 10,678 × $5.00 per million, about $0.053. In fact it costs more, about $0.068, because the tools and system part is rewritten as a 1-hour entry at 2x. That's more than ten times as much, and the same multiple applies to turns 10 and 11. Three invalidations in a row, each reasonable on its own, cost as much input as thirty steady turns.

The design lessons follow directly.

  • Load all tools the agent might need at the start, rather than adding them mid-task. (Or use the docs' tool-addition mechanism, still beta.)
  • Keep the system prompt immutable within a conversation, and put changing guidance in the messages.
  • Choose effort and speed per conversation, not per turn.
  • Attach images where they're needed, knowing that the first attachment costs one messages rewrite.
d736ac629a:
Turn 10 also shows why breakpoint T exists. Entries are only stored where breakpoints are placed. So without a breakpoint on the tool list, the system edit would have rewritten tools too. With it, the roughly 740-token tool prefix survives.

That only works because the tool prefix is above the 512-token minimum. An earlier version of the example had shorter tool descriptions, about 380 tokens. There, the T breakpoint silently wrote nothing, and turn 10 read zero. A breakpoint on a prefix below the minimum isn't an error. It's just inert, and only the usage counters reveal it.
927fcae68c:
The break-even arithmetic is short enough to do in an exam.

With a 5-minute cache, two calls cost 1.25 + 0.05 = 1.3 units of prefix instead of 2. So caching pays from the first reuse. With a 1-hour cache, two calls cost 2.05 against 2. So it pays from the second reuse within the hour.

If the prefix is used at least every five minutes, the 5-minute cache stays warm for free. It's cheaper than the 1-hour TTL only by the one-off difference in write price (the arithmetic below makes this precise).

The 1-hour TTL wins when the gap between uses is between 5 and 60 minutes. Take an internal tool used every 20 minutes. It rewrites a 5-minute entry on every call, at 1.25 each. A 1-hour entry costs 2 once per hour, plus 0.05 per read. For gaps over an hour, neither TTL helps much. Example 09 runs this sweep.
d4606ff1b1:
The break-even rules above assume regular gaps. Real traffic is irregular. A slightly more general model gives a rule you can apply to any prefix.

Assume requests sharing a prefix arrive at random, at an average rate of λ per minute. That's a Poisson process, the standard first model for independent arrivals. It's the same assumption behind Erlang formulas in telecom capacity planning. The chance that the gap since the previous request exceeds T minutes is e−λT.

Every read refreshes the entry. So a request reads if the gap was within the TTL, and rewrites otherwise. The expected prefix cost per request, in units of the base input price, is then:
4bc6b46d0d:
Solve for the break-even points and you get two numbers worth remembering. A 1-hour cache pays for itself above about 0.7 requests per hour on that prefix. A 5-minute cache pays above about 2.8 per hour. At high rates both converge to the read price, because both stay permanently warm.

That corrects a common simplification, including one earlier in this section. For a stable prefix with steady traffic, the 5-minute TTL isn't meaningfully cheaper than the 1-hour TTL. The only difference is the write premium on the rare cold start. The real cost of the 1-hour TTL shows up somewhere else: in prefixes that keep growing.
3bb3f0c786:
A moving checkpoint writes new blocks every turn. So the write premium is paid every turn, not once.

Take a conversation with H cached history tokens that adds D new tokens per turn. Let p be the share of user pauses longer than five minutes. With a 5-minute checkpoint, a turn costs p·1.25·H + (1−p)·r·H + 1.25·D. With a 1-hour checkpoint (pauses under an hour), it costs r·H + 2·D. The 1-hour checkpoint wins once p > 0.75·D / ((1.25 − r)·H).

For a 40,000-token history growing 1,500 tokens per turn, that threshold is only 2.3%. If more than one pause in forty exceeds five minutes, the 1-hour checkpoint is cheaper. One expired 5-minute entry costs a rewrite of the entire history.

An agent loop with no human in it makes tool calls every few seconds. There p is near zero, and the 5-minute checkpoint wins by 0.75·D per turn.

Example 22 prints both models. It also replays a bursty gap pattern: bursts of five calls 25 minutes apart. There the 1-hour TTL costs 0.05 units per request, against 0.29 for the 5-minute one.
118e12cc0f:
The minimum cacheable length is a property of the model. It applies to the prefix up to each breakpoint, and falling short is silent. Three quick cases cover the exam's range.

  • A 3,000-token system prompt on Haiku 4.5 (minimum 4,096) is never cached. Both cache counters are zero on every request, and the full price is paid, with no error.
  • The same prompt on Haiku 5.5 (minimum 512) caches from the first reuse, at 0.1x read price.
  • A 400-token tool list with its own breakpoint on Opus 5.5 is inert on its own. But the system breakpoint after it covers tools plus system, which is well above 512. So the tools are still cached as part of that longer prefix. The separate tools breakpoint only matters if you want tools to survive a system edit (section 16). Then it must cover at least 512 tokens.

The diagnostic is the same in every case. If a request you meant to cache shows zero in both counters, compare the prefix length at each breakpoint with the model's minimum. Do that before looking for anything subtler.
c9b645d5a6:
A conversation or agent loop resends its entire history every turn. So the history is the largest and fastest-growing prefix.

Caching only the system prompt (a breakpoint that never moves) means every turn pays full price for every earlier turn. Cost grows quadratically with turns. Cache checkpointing means moving a breakpoint to the end of the conversation on every request. Turn n reads the prefix that turn n−1 wrote, and pays full price only for the new blocks.
8398509c59:
There are two ways to implement it.

Automatic caching (top-level cache_control) moves the breakpoint for you. It's the simplest correct answer.

Explicit checkpointing strips the old marker from history and puts one on the last block each turn. Use it when you need a second breakpoint on the stable system prompt with a different TTL, or when a platform doesn't support automatic caching. Don't accumulate markers on every turn. The limit is four.
23315f0fad:
In example 10's twelve-turn agent, a system-only breakpoint gets a 36% token hit rate. A moving checkpoint, automatic or explicit, reaches 87% and costs under a third as much.

Four things break checkpointing in practice.

  • Editing history: pruning old tool results or summarising (chapter 16's compaction) rewrites the prefix from the edit point. Do it rarely and in large steps, and expect one full write afterwards.
  • Dropping or altering thinking blocks: pass them back unchanged. On the 5.5 models a dropped thinking block invalidates the messages cache from that point. (And editing history before a thinking block can be a 400 on newer accounts.)
  • Changing effort, thinking mode or tool_choice mid-conversation: each invalidates the messages cache. Keep them constant per conversation.
  • Parallel fan-out on a cold cache: an entry is readable only after the first response starts. So ten parallel subagents sharing a 30K-token prefix all pay the write. Send one first, wait for its response to start, then send the rest (example 15: about 7x cheaper).
47d5de86f2:
For subagents (chapter 03), give each one a stable prefix of its own. Shared tools and system prompt go first, as one entry reused by every worker. The worker-specific brief comes after.

Cached content still counts toward the context window. Caching saves money and latency, not context.

Batches (chapter 07) can use caching too. But hits are best-effort, because requests run in arbitrary order and over a long window. The 1-hour TTL improves the odds.
52a1f3c953: Four breakpoints, two TTLs and the rule "stable first, volatile last" combine into a small set of layouts. Those layouts cover most applications. Learning them as patterns is faster than re-deriving them, and exam scenarios usually describe one of these shapes.
277c1cdce6:
Java developers have met this design before, as the JDBC prepared-statement cache. A driver caches the parsed plan keyed by the SQL text. So "SELECT ... WHERE id = " + id creates a new entry per request and never hits. "SELECT ... WHERE id = ?" with a bound parameter hits every time.

Prompt caching is the same discipline at a larger scale. The cached prefix is the statement text. Everything that varies per request must be a "bound parameter" placed after the last breakpoint. A timestamp in the system prompt is string-concatenated SQL.

The analogy also explains where the fix belongs: in the request builder, the one place that assembles prompts, not at each call site.
2ce4f7989c: You can't see the cache, only the usage counters. So measurement is arithmetic over logged usage. Three numbers are worth a dashboard.
0a59dfa235:
Read the numbers together.

  • A request hit rate near 100% with a modest token hit rate means the stable prefix is cached but the conversation isn't. Add a moving checkpoint.
  • A request hit rate of zero after a deploy means something now varies inside the cached prefix. Diff two consecutive rendered requests up to the first breakpoint, exactly as chapter 12 diffs prompts.
  • A high write ratio with steady traffic means the TTL is shorter than the gap between uses, or the breakpoint sits on a block that changes.
  • Both counters at zero means not cached at all: below the minimum length, no breakpoint, or a different workspace.
387ee2349d: Make cache behaviour testable offline. Write a unit test that sends two identical requests through a fake client. Assert that the second one reads more than 90% of its input. That catches the timestamp-in-the-prompt regression before it reaches the invoice. The companion's cachesim.py is such a fake, and any test of the request builder can use it.
ccd9432344: Most cache problems leave a recognisable signature in the per-request counters. Learn the signatures, and diagnosis becomes a lookup. The examples assume a 6,000-token stable prefix and a conversation growing by about 800 tokens per turn.
8e5a6d5ed6:
Make the signatures testable. The cheapest regression test for caching sends two consecutive requests, built by your real request builder, through a fake client that implements the caching rules. Then it asserts on the counters.

It runs in milliseconds and needs no API key. And it fails on the day someone adds a build id to the system prompt, not on the day the invoice arrives.
b3f1b9e03c: Writes every time with no reads means each request has a new prefix. The volatile values at the top make every key unique. A longer TTL (A) doesn't make different prefixes match. More breakpoints (C) would all sit after the changing first line. D is irrelevant.
34755a476c: Each of the three settings is a documented 400 on the 5.5 models. 400s are never transient (C). Aliases (D) don't change request validation, and they add drift. A migration is a checklist plus measurement. It isn't a reason to stay on an old model (A).
594c89aef7: Model choice is per step, and by measurement. Triage likely passes on Haiku. Diagnosis may need Opus. A ignores quality. C truncates answers and thinking. D is right only for work nobody waits for (chapter 07), and triage in a live support flow isn't that.
800f40d286: The history is never cached, because no breakpoint covers it. A moving checkpoint does. A doesn't cover the history. C rewrites the prefix every turn, so it never hits. D exceeds the four-breakpoint limit.
c604d1553d: The gap is on the output side. Price output_tokens, which includes thinking (output_tokens_details.thinking_tokens shows how much), and control it with effort. There's no long-context surcharge on 4.6+ models except Haiku 5.5 (C). A and D are small, and on the input side.
40ef641230: For agentic work, the unit of value is a resolved task. Failures carry costs far larger than tokens (section 04, case B). A is false (same read multiplier). C is false (same 1M window). D is wrong for interactive agent loops.
237e0ee6d1: Self-reported confidence separates right from wrong answers poorly, so wrong answers pass the gate. A validator gate keeps most of the saving at near-large-model quality (section 05, example 17). B is the same broken signal. C makes it worse. D gives up the saving for no reason.
4735348c25: Effort is rendered into the prompt, so each change rewrites the messages segment (section 15, trace in section 16). A doesn't stop invalidation. C exceeds four breakpoints. D gives up the reads without fixing the cause. If you need two effort levels, split the work into two conversations or steps, each with constant settings.
f6c20877f9: A full cost model is built line by line from realistic usage records (section 11). A ignores input, caching and thinking. C uses the wrong workload shape. D isn't a forecast. Writing the assumptions down turns the forecast into monitoring targets.
